title: Your charity

lines: A JAR BETWEEN THE RICE AND THE TEA.
cards: On a kitchen shelf, between the rice and the tea, sits an old jam jar with a strip of tape on it. Someone has written one word on the tape in marker: sadaqah.

Every evening, whoever empties their pockets drops in the loose change. Nobody makes a speech about it. Once a month the jar is emptied and the money goes somewhere: a food bank, a neighbor's medical bill, a well.
The jar isn't impressive. It's just always there, filling slowly. You met the word on day one hundred forty-nine.

teach.b: First, two gifts. Zakat is the required one: a set share of wealth, owed by those who have enough, to the groups the Qur'an names. Sadaqah is the open one: voluntary, no minimum, given at any hour.
Surah al-Baqarah praises those who spend their wealth by night and by day, in secret and in the open, and says their reward is with their Lord. Not one event, but a pattern running through the hours.
That's the case for the jar: a small gift that keeps going shapes the giver in a way a single grand gesture may not. The size of it?
Earlier in the same surah, the Qur'an compares money spent in Allah's way to a single grain that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each ear: something small put in the ground and multiplied.
The same surah says giving openly is good, and giving quietly to the poor is better for you. So a regular, quiet gift has two things going for it at once. And what counts?

teach.h: EVERY GOOD DEED IS A CHARITY.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says every good deed is a charity.
Another hadith in Bukhari names some: a good word, helping someone onto their mount, removing something harmful from the road. Sadaqah is wider than money.
A regular sadaqah can be a monthly transfer, a weekly visit, or a jar of coins. What matters is that it comes back around.

how: Alongside the required zakat, Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in any amount and at any time; some set up a regular gift, weekly or monthly, following surah al-Baqarah's praise of those who give by night and by day.

o: a regular sadaqah, small enough to keep, given again and again
the zakat you owe once a year on the savings you hold
a large gift given once, in public, to a well-known cause

p: seven ears, a hundred grains each

s: in Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet says every good deed is a charity.
surah al-Baqarah praises those who give by night and by day
it praises those who spend by night and by day, in secret and in the open (2:274).
zakat and sadaqah are the same thing
zakat is the required share; sadaqah is voluntary and open, in any amount, at any time.

games.q: you have a little to give. you could give it all at once, once a year, or a small amount every week. which fits al-Baqarah's picture of the giver?
o: the gift that runs through the weeks.
games.why: al-Baqarah praises those who spend by night and by day, in secret and in the open (2:274): giving as a pattern, not one event. a jar of coins qualifies.

practice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and notice how little effort it takes to hold them open.

Think of what you could give regularly without strain, a small amount each week, an hour of time, a meal for someone, small enough that you'd never skip it, and let one place it could go settle in your mind.
If you pray, ask Allah to accept it.

wordCard.voice: Your charity. A regular sadaqah, small enough to keep, given again and again, quietly. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: voluntary charity, given at any time.

carryVoice: Your line: regular giving. The rhythm of a gift matters more than its size. Go gently.
